title: Mira's Lord
hookLine: a song closes by saying whose it is: the women who signed their own names, and the names they signed
carry: in bhakti, the song belongs to god

cards: Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar. Mira's Lord is Giridhar, the one who lifted the mountain. That phrase closes song after song sung in Mirabai's name, like a stamp pressed into wax.
Singers call it a chhap. Yesterday's women were given their words by the poets of the epics.
The next stretch of the year turned to women whose own words survive, in songs and in a few lines of scripture, sometimes with their names pressed right into them.

teach.b: This is bhakti, the path of loving devotion, in the words of women who lived it. In bhakti, God isn't an idea to be proved. God is someone you love, by a name you choose and keep repeating.

teach.h: THE NAMES THEY GAVE THEIR GOD.
teach.b: So start with the names they gave their God. Mira's songs end on Giridhar. Akka Mahadevi, in Karnataka, closes her vachanas on the lord white as jasmine.
Andal, in Tamil, dreams her whole wedding to the Lord, verse by verse.

Then the names they gave themselves. Karaikkal Ammaiyar's tradition says Shiva called her Mother. But in her own hymns she signs as a pey, a ghoul of the cremation ground, dancing near him in the night.
She didn't hide the bones. She signed with them. Lal Ded, in Kashmir, let people curse her and others bring her flowers, and said neither could touch her.
And some women left questions instead of songs, kept in an Upanishad. Gargi asks Yajnavalkya what the world is woven on, and when she's told to stop, she comes back later with two more.

Maitreyi, offered property, asks what she'd do with something that can't make her immortal. One honest turn. With songs that traveled mouth to mouth, nobody can always say which lines go back to the woman herself.
Either way, the signature keeps working.
Whoever sings a Mira bhajan at a home shrine today steps aside at the end: not my Lord, but Mira's Lord.

teach.h: NOT MY LORD, BUT MIRA'S LORD.
teach.b: Many devotees put it this way: you borrow a saint's love for God, until one morning it's your own.

how: The songs of women saints such as Mirabai, Andal and Akka Mahadevi are still sung in homes, temples and gatherings, and some Sri Vaishnava families sing Andal's wedding song at their own weddings.

o: a list of saints read aloud on a festival day
a seal stamped in wax on a king's royal letters
a look back from the top at the women's own signed words

games.q: the women and their signatures — tap the pairs.
p: signs as a ghoul of the cremation ground
asks for what can't die, not property

s: Karaikkal Ammaiyar signs her hymns as Mother
Mother is the name tradition says Shiva gave her; she signs as a pey, a ghoul of the cremation ground.
Gargi is told to stop asking, and comes back later with two more questions
she pictures herself like a warrior stringing a bow.
everyone agrees which Mira songs go back to Mira herself
some readers sort older from newer; others say a song lives by being sung.

games.q: you're Mirabai in Vrindavan. you ask to meet a holy man, and word comes back: he has vowed not to see women. what do you send back?
o: an angry letter about his vow.
one sentence: I thought there was only one man in Vrindavan, Krishna.
games.why: in the story, Mira says she thought Krishna was the only man in Vrindavan, and the renunciant comes out to meet her. it's told about her, not recorded at the door.

practice: Choose one name for God that you love, or one these women used: Giridhar, Krishna, Shiva, the Lord. Say it silently on each out-breath, the way a bhakti song comes back to the name at its close.
When the mind wanders, come back to the name, without scolding yourself. If you don't pray, rest on a word that means love to you, or simply on the breath.

wordCard.voice: The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the women in their own words, and the names they signed. Today's word.

orig.note: Hindi, in Devanagari: chhāp, a stamp, the closing name that tells you whose song it is.

carryVoice: Your line: in bhakti, the song belongs to God. The name at the end tells you whose it is. Rest well.

sources.ref: Songs attributed to Mirabai (the closing line 'Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar')
Vachanas of Akka Mahadevi (the signature 'lord white as jasmine', Chennamallikarjuna)
Karaikkal Ammaiyar, Tiruvalankattu Mutta Tiruppatikam (closing signature); Periya Puranam (her life)
